client: Lately, I’ve been feeling completely overwhelmed at my new job. I’m the only one on the team who doesn’t have experience in marketing, and it’s like everyone expects me to know what I’m doing right away. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like the problem is just me not being good enough or prepared enough for the role.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of self-doubt in this new role. I notice you mention feeling overwhelmed while also dismissing whether therapy can help - might there be part of you that's afraid you can't succeed in this position?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I guess I am afraid of failing. Every time I try to ask questions or learn something new, I feel like I’m just exposing how clueless I am. It’s like I’m stuck in this cycle of doubting myself and then avoiding tasks because I’m scared of messing up. I don’t know if therapy can fix that—it feels like I just need to work harder or know more.
therapist: It seems like you're putting a lot of pressure on yourself to know everything right away. What would it be like to give yourself permission to be a learner in this new role, rather than expecting yourself to have all the answers immediately?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I know logically that makes sense, but it's so hard to actually feel that way. When I see my coworkers handling things so effortlessly, it just reinforces that I'm behind. I keep thinking "why can't I just get this like they do?" It feels like giving myself permission to learn would just be making excuses for not being good enough.
therapist: It sounds like there's a gap between what you know rationally and what you feel emotionally. When you compare yourself to your coworkers, what do you think they might have experienced when they were first starting out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess they probably struggled too at first... but that's hard to picture when they all seem so confident now. It's like my brain keeps telling me "they were naturally good at this, but you're not". Even if they did struggle, it feels different for me - like my case is special somehow.
therapist: It seems like there's a part of you that feels your situation is unique and more challenging than what others might have experienced. What do you think keeps you from extending the same compassion to yourself that you might extend to others in your position?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think part of me feels like if I'm too compassionate with myself, I'll just slack off and never improve. It's like I need to be hard on myself to stay motivated, even though it's exhausting. The idea of being kinder to myself feels risky, like I might lose my edge or something.
therapist: It sounds like you're worried that self-compassion might lead to complacency. Have you considered that being kinder to yourself might actually help you approach challenges with more energy and focus, rather than draining your motivation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's an interesting thought... I've never really considered that being kinder to myself could actually help me perform better. It's just so counter to how I've always operated. I guess I'm skeptical because it feels like I've gotten this far by pushing myself hard, and I'm worried that changing that approach might backfire. But I also see how exhausted I am from being so critical all the time.
therapist: I hear you wrestling with this idea - there's both skepticism about changing your approach and some openness to how it might help. What would it look like to experiment with small acts of self-kindness while maintaining your strong work ethic, rather than seeing it as an all-or-nothing choice?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess I could try small things, like not beating myself up over every mistake. But it’s hard because my first instinct is always to criticize myself when something goes wrong. I’m worried that even small acts of kindness might feel forced or fake, like I’m just pretending to be okay with messing up.
therapist: It sounds like you're willing to try small changes, yet also anticipate that being kind to yourself might feel unnatural at first. What if, instead of focusing on how genuine it feels, we simply practiced noticing those critical thoughts when they arise, without needing to change them right away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That approach feels a bit more manageable, but I’m still worried that just noticing the thoughts won’t actually help. I feel like I’ll just get stuck in this loop of being aware of my self-criticism but still feeling bad about it. Isn’t there something more proactive I can do to stop those thoughts from taking over?
therapist: It sounds like you're eager for tools to actively shift these patterns, not just observe them. What if we experimented with asking yourself, when those critical thoughts arise: "Would I speak this way to a colleague who was learning?" This might help bridge the gap between awareness and action in a concrete way.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That’s an interesting idea, but I’m not sure it would work for me. Even if I wouldn’t speak that way to a colleague, I feel like I deserve the criticism because it’s my responsibility to know this stuff. It’s like holding myself to a lower standard feels wrong, like I’m letting myself off the hook too easily.
therapist: It sounds like there's a strong belief that being hard on yourself is necessary for maintaining responsibility. What do you think might happen if you experimented with viewing self-kindness not as lowering standards, but as a different approach to meeting those same high expectations?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I’ve never really thought about it that way—as a different approach rather than lowering standards. I guess I’m worried that if I’m too kind to myself, I’ll lose my drive to improve. It’s like I’ve always believed that being harsh is what keeps me moving forward, and I’m scared that changing that might make me stagnate. But I can see how being kinder might help me feel less drained, even if it feels risky.
therapist: It sounds like you're beginning to consider new possibilities while still holding onto some understandable concerns about change. What would it be like to view self-kindness as fuel for your drive rather than something that might diminish it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
